title: Fatigue and a pulse of 28 during a heatwave

source.citation: Costantini I, Mantelli G, Carollo M, Losso L, Morando E, Bacchion M, et al. Not only Van Gogh: a case of BRASH syndrome with concomitant digoxin toxicity. J Med Case Rep. 2024;18(1):273.

presentation.hpi: Three to four days of worsening fatigue during a heatwave. Her GP found a blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg and a heart rate of 28/min and sent her straight to the ED. She has passed no urine for 3 days, and for the past week has noticed 'flashing lights and sparkles around objects'. She takes her medicines as prescribed; the last doses of digoxin, ramipril and bisoprolol were 2 hours before arrival.
pmh: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
Platelet function defect with frequent epistaxis
Atrial fibrillation; percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion 2 years ago
Mitral valve prolapse and pulmonary hypertension
Cirrhosis and ascites from congestive hepatopathy due to cor pulmonale
Iron-deficiency anemia; recent Helicobacter pylori eradication
Left mastectomy for breast cancer 7 years ago, no recurrence

exam: Respiratory distress, RR 40/min; SpO2 89% on room air
After the first round of treatment, on isoproterenol: still HR 30/min and BP 75/50 mm Hg
ecg: Idioventricular rhythm, 28/min. Later: junctional rhythm with ventricular bigeminy (day 1), atrial fibrillation with ventricular ectopics (day 3), back to baseline atrial fibrillation by day 14.

diagnosis.primary: Chronic digoxin toxicity with BRASH syndrome (bradycardia, renal failure, AV-nodal blockade, shock, hyperkalemia) after dehydration in a heatwave
differentials: Hyperkalemia from acute kidney injury alone
Inferior myocardial infarction with complete heart block

management: Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV, nebulized salbutamol 10 mg, sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 150 mL IV, and 10% dextrose 250 mL with insulin 10 units
Isoproterenol infusion from 2.5 μg/min, increased to 4 μg/min aiming for a heart rate of 45–50/min
Potassium-shifting therapy repeated without effect; urgent nephrology consultation for emergency dialysis
Empirical digoxin immune Fab, 2 vials (40 mg), then 5 more vials once the digoxin level returned
ICU: continuous venovenous hemofiltration until day 9; isoproterenol stopped on day 8
outcome: Potassium normalized on CVVH and the rhythm returned to baseline atrial fibrillation as digoxin fell over 17 days; the stay was complicated by pneumonia and epistaxis needing transfusion. Discharged after 35 days on intermittent dialysis, stopped within 3 months; stage 3b chronic kidney disease at 6 months.
teachingPoints: BRASH (bradycardia, renal failure, AV-nodal blockade, shock, hyperkalemia) is a vicious cycle: dehydration and AKI raise potassium and AV-nodal drug levels, which worsen bradycardia and renal perfusion.
Digoxin is renally cleared, so AKI in a patient taking it causes chronic toxicity; ask about nausea, confusion and visual change (flashing lights, halos, yellow-green vision).

Give digoxin-specific Fab for life-threatening arrhythmia or bradycardia, severe hyperkalemia, or end-organ dysfunction, without waiting for a level; in chronic toxicity, vials ≈ serum digoxin (ng/mL) × weight (kg) / 100.
Dialysis does not remove digoxin (large volume of distribution) but treats refractory hyperkalemia and anuria.
After Fab, routine immunoassays measure total (free plus bound) digoxin, so levels cannot guide further dosing; follow the ECG, potassium and clinical state.

questions.q: Besides hyperkalemia, which process most likely contributes to this presentation?
questions.extra: ABG: pH 7.10, PaCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3⁻ 10 mmol/L, lactate normal, K⁺ 8.9 mmol/L. ECG: idioventricular rhythm, 28/min.
options: Inferior myocardial infarction with heart block
Digoxin accumulation from acute kidney injury
Septic shock from a urinary source
questions.explanation: Dehydration in a heatwave, on ramipril, spironolactone and furosemide, caused anuric AKI; renally cleared digoxin accumulated and, with bisoprolol, drove the BRASH cycle. A week of 'flashing lights and sparkles' points to digoxin toxicity, and her level was 13.7 μg/L. Normal lactate argues against septic shock.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.extra: Repeat ABG: K⁺ 9.3 mmol/L after two rounds of calcium chloride, insulin–dextrose, nebulized salbutamol and sodium bicarbonate. HR 30/min, BP 75/50 mm Hg on isoproterenol. Anuric for 3 days.
options: Digoxin-specific Fab now, with emergency dialysis for the potassium
Hemodialysis alone, which will also clear the digoxin
Transvenous pacing, withholding any further calcium
Atropine 1 mg, repeated to a total of 3 mg
questions.explanation: In a patient on digoxin with AKI, refractory hyperkalemia and a bradyarrhythmia, give digoxin-specific Fab empirically: it reverses Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase blockade, lowering potassium and improving conduction. Dialysis is still needed for the potassium and anuria but does not remove digoxin. Pacing does not treat the hyperkalemia and can provoke arrhythmias in digoxin toxicity.

questions.q: After 7 vials of Fab, the measured serum digoxin is 10.0 μg/L at 6 h and above 10 μg/L at the next check. How should this be interpreted?
questions.extra: Digoxin 13.7 μg/L on arrival, before Fab. On CVVH. Next day: K⁺ 4.96 mmol/L; ECG junctional rhythm with ventricular bigeminy.
options: Fab has failed, so the full calculated dose is now needed
Ongoing absorption of the dose taken 2 h before arrival
CVVH is releasing digoxin from tissue stores
The assay measures total digoxin, including Fab-bound drug
questions.explanation: Routine immunoassays do not separate free from Fab-bound digoxin, so total levels stay high or rise after Fab and cannot guide further dosing. Follow the ECG, potassium and clinical state instead; here she needed no further Fab, and the rhythm improved as potassium normalized.

questions.q: She received IV calcium chloride before digoxin toxicity was suspected. What does the evidence suggest?
options: Available data do not show that it increases arrhythmias or death
It is absolutely contraindicated because of the 'stone heart' risk
It inactivates digoxin-specific Fab given afterwards
It raises serum digoxin by displacing it from tissue binding
questions.explanation: The 'stone heart' warning rests on old animal data and case reports; a retrospective human series found no excess dysrhythmias or deaths when calcium was given in digoxin toxicity, and none occurred here. Calcium does not affect Fab or digoxin levels, but Fab, not calcium, is the specific treatment for digoxin-related hyperkalemia.

evidence.quote: We present the case of a 66-year-old Caucasian female patient who consulted her general practitioner (GP) during a heatwave owing to worsening fatigue over the past 3–4 days.
she was found to be hypotensive (80/40 mmHg) and bradycardic (28 bpm), prompting immediate referral to the emergency department (ED)
she disclosed being anuric for the past 3 days and experiencing visual phenomena such as "flashing lights and sparkles around objects" over the previous week
she confirmed adherence to her medication regimen, noting that her last doses of digoxin, ramipril, and bisoprolol were taken 2 hours before arrival
The patient had a medical history of Osler Weber Rendu syndrome, characterized by pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
had undergone a left mastectomy for breast cancer 7 years prior, with subsequent negative follow-ups
she had a platelet function deficit … and was experiencing frequent epistaxis

Her medical history also included hypertension, atrial fibrillation—treated with percutaneous occlusion of the atrial appendage 2 years earlier—mitral valve prolapse, pulmonary hypertension, iron deficiency anemia
recent eradication of Helicobacter pylori infection, hepatic cirrhosis, and ascites secondary to congestive hepatopathy attributed to cor pulmonale
Pharmacological history included digoxin at 0.25 mg once per day, bisoprolol at 5 mg twice per day, ramipril at 2.5 mg once per day
spironolactone at 25 mg once per day, furosemide at 25 mg once per day, and pravastatin at 40 mg once per day

by day 14, the ECG returned to atrial fibrillation (the patient's baseline
Laboratory tests disclosed a serum digoxin level of 13.7 μg/L, a creatinine level of 8.11 mg/dL, and a potassium level of 8.64 mmol/L.

evidence.quote: The serum digoxin levels gradually decreased to 1.38 μg/L over 17 days.
treatment was initiated with 10 mL of 10% intravenous calcium chloride, 10 mg of nebulized salbutamol, an infusion of isoproterenol at a rate of 2.5 μg/min
150 mL of 8.4% intravenous bicarbonate, and 250 mL of 10% dextrose in water (DW10%) with 10 units of insulin
the isoproterenol infusion was titrated up to 4 μg/minute aiming to achieve a heart rate of 45–50 bpm
The antikalemic treatment was repeated without success, leading to an urgent consultation with a nephrologist for emergency dialysis.
Given the suspicion of concomitant digoxin toxicity, empirical treatment with digoxin immune fab was initiated, administering 40 mg via two vials.
After administering an additional five vials of digoxin immune fab, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU)

evidence.quote: continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) was promptly initiated, leading to an improvement in serum potassium levels to 4.96 mmol/L the following day
she continued with CVVH until day 9; the isoproterenol infusion was ceased on day 8
We hypothesize that the syndrome was triggered by initial dehydration, exacerbated by the high temperatures
The hospitalization was further complicated by pneumonia and multiple episodes of epistaxis, necessitating blood transfusions.
The patient was discharged after 35 days in good condition, albeit still requiring intermittent dialysis.
Kidney function gradually improved over 3 months, during which the frequency of dialysis was reduced from three times per week to two and then discontinued.
At 6 months of follow-up, the patient was diagnosed with stage IIIb chronic kidney disease
